chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
title: Morris French, the legless pianist Penny, and jam sessions
summary: Older trumpeter Morris French and pianist Penny, who lost his legs at Lutcher, played that first job; the young players also went out jamming to get hired.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well, I was going to ask, who else was in that band at the Gypsy Key Room? How many musicians did you have?
Well, that night I started, I started one of the old timers, I must say. His name was Morris French. Oh, yeah.

Great tramp-owner. Great tramp-owner player. And I had him there, start out with, because I always take the older fellow with me on everything, because I figured like that, well, he knew. Yeah. You ought to have somebody as a guide, you know. Well, I took him, and another fellow played piano by the name of Penny, and another young fellow with me. I started at the same time, the name was Dick, and the boy played the drum. We had the two older ones, well, they kept us in line. And from that on, well, they began to give us a little job, and we just kept going.
Morris French and who else was there over?

Morris French and another little fellow by the name of Penny, Penny, Penny, Penny, piano player. Little fellow didn't have no legs. Oh, yeah. But he would get on the stool and spin around. Really? He belonged to Fifth Baptist Church now. Oh, he's still alive.

What was the legs he had, you know? You don't know his real name. Well, we always named him, called him by Penny, Penny, Penny, yeah, Penny. I forget his real name, but he used to come to the house a lot.
Is he uptown here or something like that?
He's still up here yet. Still up here yet. And that's what, all the city was talking about him at one time. Oh, yeah?
Yeah. I wish I could hear anything. Is he still playing, you think? I bet he's getting to the house. Well, I know he's in church.
I don't know if he's playing there, but when he was playing, he was there. Yeah. Yeah, he was there.
Did he have an accident or something?

Well, yeah, that happened in Lutcher. Yeah, that happened in Lutcher. It happened in what you call the sugar cane car up there, you know, that. Lumber mill, whatever, that fire, you know, up there. He happened to hop on there and got both his legs cut off. Yeah. He still was all right, the young brother. He'd get around on them clutches and hop around good. And still get around on them now. Get around on them all. Get up there on that piano there and show up. If anybody didn't tell you had no legs, you wouldn't know. He'd be spinning around there and play a nice piano. But we had several groups and like I said, we'd always form up a lot of groups and so forth. Like the fellow knew one from another. And then we would go out jam, what you call jam section. If a fellow wouldn't have a job, well, we'd take our instrument anyhow. And we'd go out jam section. If a fellow would play, well, we'd go and set in. All that was a good recreation and then let the other fellow see what we could do. Then the problem when the fellow got void, well, they would hire you when they see what you could do. We would always go out, whatever, we'd call jam section to come. And then some folks would knock off from one job to another and then they'd go jam section.
